(CNN) -- Texas authorities released court documents Thursday detailing the items seized from the medical office and storage unit of Dr. Conrad Murray, the cardiologist who was with Michael Jackson when he fell ill and died on June 25. Dr. Conrad Murray's office was searched Wednesday for "evidence of the offense of manslaughter." Detectives searched both sites in Houston on Wednesday for "evidence of the offense of manslaughter," according to court documents. Murray's attorney confirmed the search Wednesday. Among the items removed from Murray's office were a computer; 27 tablets of Phentermine, a prescription-strength appetite suppressant; 1 tablet of clonazepam, an anti-anxiety medication; and some Rolodex cards. From Murray's storage unit, authorities removed two computer hard drives; an "important contact list"; a suspension notice from Houston's Doctors Hospital; notices from the Internal Revenue Service; and a list of medical and hospital documents. Jackson's former nurse, Cherilyn Lee, was also approached on Wednesday by investigators who wanted copies of medical files she had on the singer, Lee told CNN's Nancy Grace. Lee said she handed over the files to officials with the coroner's office. Ed Chernoff, a Houston lawyer hired by Murray soon after Jackson's death, confirmed that Los Angeles Police detectives and federal Drug Enforcement Administration agents used a search warrant to enter Murray's office in northeast Houston on Wednesday morning. "The search warrant authorized law enforcement to search for and seize items, including documents, they believed constituted evidence of the offense of manslaughter," Chernoff said in a written statement Wednesday. Chernoff said members of Murray's legal team were at the medical office during the search, which he said "was conducted by members of the DEA, two robbery-homicide detectives from the Los Angeles Police Department and Houston Police officers." "Law enforcement concluded their search around 12:30 p.m. and left with a forensic image of a business computer hard drive and 21 documents. None of the documents taken had previously been requested by law enforcement or the L.A. coroner's office," Chernoff said. Tammy Kidd, a spokeswoman at Chernoff's office, said the search "was absolutely a surprise to us, because we've had open lines of communication this whole time." "Based on Dr. Murray's minute-by-minute and item-by-item description of Michael Jackson's last days, he should not be a target of criminal charges," Chernoff said Tuesday. "Dr. Murray was the last doctor standing when Michael Jackson died and it seems all the fury is directed toward him." Los Angeles investigators have interviewed Murray twice, Chernoff said. A third interview has not been scheduled, he said. Police impounded his car, which had been parked at Jackson's Holmby Hills home, the night after Jackson's death. It was released to Murray several days later. "Dr. Murray is frustrated by negative and often erroneous media reports. He has to walk around 24-7 with a bodyguard," Chernoff said. "He can't operate his practice. He can't go to work because he is harassed no matter where he goes." At least two investigations are under way into Jackson's death. The Los Angeles County coroner is waiting for toxicology results to determine a cause of death, while the city Police Department, with assistance from the Drug Enforcement Administration, is looking at the possibility of criminal charges. A coroner's office spokesman said the autopsy findings could be released in the next week or more. Los Angeles Police Chief William Bratton told CNN he would wait for the coroner to determine the exact cause of Jackson's death. "And based on those, we will have an idea of what it is we are dealing (with): Are we dealing with a homicide, or are we dealing with an accidental overdose?" he said. CNN's Alan Duke, Ted Rowlands and Randi Kaye contributed to this report.

**Uncovering the Evidence: Inside the Law Enforcement Raids on Dr. Conrad Murray**

Following the sudden and tragic death of global pop icon Michael Jackson on June 25, 2009, public shock quickly transformed into an intense, high-stakes criminal investigation. As details surrounding the 50-year-old performer's final hours began to emerge, law enforcement scrutiny turned almost immediately to Dr. Conrad Murray, a cardiologist hired through AEG Live to serve as Jackson’s personal physician during preparations for his upcoming "This Is It" comeback tour. What initially appeared to be a medical emergency rapidly evolved into a homicide probe, with authorities focusing on the potential offense of involuntary manslaughter.

On July 22, 2009, the investigation reached a major turning point when a joint task force—comprising Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) homicide detectives, agents from the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), and local Houston police officers—executed a series of coordinated search warrants in Houston, Texas. The primary targets of the federal and local raid were Dr. Murray’s primary practice, the Armstrong Medical Clinic, and a nearby public storage unit he had rented.

The atmosphere at the clinic was tense as armed officers secured the premises, cordoned off the area, and spent hours meticulously sifting through the physician's professional and personal records. The objective was to establish a clear timeline of Murray’s treatment of Jackson, trace the procurement of powerful medical drugs, and determine whether the doctor had displayed gross negligence in his care of the pop star.

The haul from the search was extensive, yielding vital physical, digital, and documentary evidence that would form the bedrock of the prosecution's case. Among the items seized were multiple computer hard drives, flash drives, and cell phone records, which investigators hoped would reveal communications between Murray, Jackson, and pharmaceutical suppliers. 

Crucially, officers also confiscated a vast array of medical documents, including patient charts, billing records, and personal notes. Among these papers, investigators discovered hospital suspension notices—administrative documents indicating that Murray’s staff privileges at certain medical facilities had lapsed or been suspended, primarily due to delinquent medical records and unpaid dues. These documents provided crucial context regarding Murray's professional standing and mounting financial troubles at the time he was treating Jackson.

In addition to documentation, authorities removed several boxes of prescription medications and medical equipment. Investigators were particularly focused on tracing the origin of Propofol—a potent, short-acting intravenous anesthetic typically reserved for surgical settings—along with various strong sedatives, such as lorazepam and midazolam. The autopsy later confirmed that Jackson died from acute Propofol intoxication, compounded by a lethal cocktail of benzodiazepines, administered in a non-hospital environment without adequate monitoring or resuscitation equipment.

The evidence secured during the Houston raids allowed prosecutors to piece together how Murray had acquired massive quantities of surgical-grade anesthetics and shipped them to his girlfriend's residence in California before administering them to Jackson as a sleep aid.

Ultimately, the physical and documentary evidence gathered from Murray’s clinic and storage unit proved decisive. It exposed severe breaches of the medical standard of care and shattered any defense that Jackson's death was a self-inflicted accident beyond the doctor's control. Less than two years after the Houston searches, Dr. Conrad Murray was formally charged, tried, and convicted of involuntary manslaughter in November 2011, serving two years of a four-year prison sentence.

**Federal agents search Michael Jackson doctor's Houston office, storage unit**

By CNN Staff
July 22, 2009 

**HOUSTON (CNN)** — Federal drug agents and Los Angeles police detectives raided the Houston medical office and a storage facility belonging to Dr. Conrad Murray on Wednesday, dramatically escalating the investigation into the death of pop star Michael Jackson.

The searches at Murray’s Armstrong Medical Clinic and a nearby storage unit mark the most aggressive public step yet by law enforcement officers trying to determine if criminal charges, including involuntary manslaughter, should be filed in connection with Jackson's June 25 death.

Dozens of law enforcement officers—including agents from the Drug Enforcement Administration, detectives from the Los Angeles Police Department, and local Harris County sheriff's deputies—converged on the medical clinic in northeast Houston shortly after 8:00 a.m. local time. 

Hours later, officers served a second search warrant at a local storage facility linked to Murray, according to law enforcement officials.

"The search warrant authorized law enforcement to search for and seize items, including medical records, that they believe constitute evidence of the offense of manslaughter," Murray’s lead attorney, Ed Chernoff, said in a statement posted on his firm’s website.

Chernoff added that the search caught the defense team by surprise, but emphasized that Murray continues to cooperate fully with investigators. "Dr. Murray was present during the search and assisted the officers," Chernoff said.

### Focus turns to powerful sedatives

According to officials familiar with the investigation, authorities were searching for evidence of controlled substances, specifically the powerful surgical anesthetic propofol, sold under the brand name Diprivan. 

Propofol, normally restricted to hospital settings for inducing anesthesia during surgery, was reportedly found in Jackson’s rented Holmby Hills estate following his death. Medical experts say the drug requires continuous monitoring of a patient's heart rate and breathing, as an overdose can cause fatal respiratory arrest.

Law enforcement sources tell CNN that investigators are working under the theory that propofol was administered to Jackson as a sleep aid in the hours leading up to his cardiac arrest, and that Murray was the physician who provided it.

Witnesses at the scene in Houston reported seeing agents carry out several boxes of documents, a computer tower, and rolling storage bins from the clinic. Search warrants in Texas remain sealed, and LAPD officials declined to comment on specific items seized during Wednesday's operations, citing an ongoing investigation.

### A deepening investigation

Murray, 56, a cardiologist licensed in Texas, California, and Nevada, was hired in May to serve as Jackson’s personal physician as the 50-year-old "King of Pop" prepared for a grueling series of 50 comeback concerts in London. 

Murray was with Jackson when he collapsed in his bed on the morning of June 25. According to Chernoff, Murray performed CPR on Jackson and called for paramedics. Jackson was later pronounced dead at Ronald Reagan UCLA Medical Center.

LAPD detectives have already interviewed Murray twice. While police have maintained that Murray is not formally named as a suspect, court filings associated with Wednesday's raids explicitly cited manslaughter as the underlying charge being investigated.

"We are seeking information directly related to the medical care provided to Michael Jackson," LAPD spokesman Officer Richard French said Wednesday. "Because this is an open homicide investigation, we cannot discuss specific evidence."

The Los Angeles County Coroner's office has completed an autopsy on Jackson's body, but the official cause of death has been held pending the results of comprehensive toxicology tests. Those results are expected to be released in the coming weeks.

As agents wrapped up their search of the Houston storage unit late Wednesday afternoon, a small crowd of onlookers and media gathered outside. Murray left the clinic in a private vehicle without taking questions from reporters.

*CNN's Ted Rowlands, Alan Duke, and Kyung Lah contributed to this report.*

counterfactuals.output:
Following the death of Michael Jackson on June 25, 2009, law enforcement agencies (including the LAPD, DEA, and local authorities) conducted high-profile raids in late July and August 2009 on Dr. Conrad Murray’s medical offices and storage facilities in **Houston, Texas**, and **Las Vegas, Nevada**.

Here is a summary of what police seized during those raids and how Murray’s lead defense attorney, **Ed Chernoff**, responded at the time.

---

### **1. What Police Seized from Murray’s Offices and Properties**

Search warrants were issued specifically seeking evidence related to **involuntary manslaughter** and the procurement and administration of powerful anesthetics, primarily **Propofol (Diprivan)**. 

The items seized included:

*   **Medications and Medical Supplies:**
    *   Multiple vials of **Propofol** (the surgical anesthetic that caused Jackson’s death).
    *   Other strong sedatives and controlled substances, including **Valium (diazepam), Lorazepam (Ativan), Midazolam (Versed)**, and **Flumazenil** (a drug used to reverse the effects of sedatives).
    *   Medical equipment, tubing, and IV bags.
*   **Digital Evidence:**
    *   Multiple computer hard drives and cell phones.
    *   Flash drives, CD-ROMs, and office computers.
    *   Emails and digital correspondence.
*   **Documents and Records:**
    *   Michael Jackson’s medical records and chart history.
    *   Billing records, client lists, and appointment calendars.
    *   Shipping receipts and invoices showing how and where pharmaceutical drugs were ordered and delivered (specifically tracking shipments sent to Murray’s girlfriend's home in Santa Monica).
    *   Storage unit rental agreements and bank records.
*   **Personal Items and Notes:**
    *   A handwritten notepad.
    *   Rolodexes and business cards.

---

### **2. What Conrad Murray’s Lawyer Had to Say**

At the time of the raids, Murray’s primary defense attorney, **Ed Chernoff**, released several public statements addressing the police actions, the seizures, and Murray's involvement:

*   **On the Raids Being "Unnecessary":** 
    Chernoff publicly stated that the raids were an overreaction and unnecessary because Dr. Murray was fully cooperating with authorities. He noted that Murray had already voluntarily given a three-hour interview to the LAPD, handed over medical records, and turned over a bag containing medications (including Propofol) from his car shortly after Jackson died.
*   **On Murray's Role in Jackson's Death:** 
    Chernoff repeatedly maintained that Murray did **not** administer the lethal dose of Propofol that killed Jackson. He stated that Murray was actually trying to *wean* Jackson off the drug, which Jackson called his "milk" to treat severe insomnia.
*   **The Defense Narrative (Self-Administration Theory):** 
    Chernoff claimed that on the morning of Jackson’s death, Murray had given Jackson a small dose of Propofol (25 mg) along with other sedatives over several hours, which was not enough to kill him. Chernoff asserted that Murray left the bedroom briefly to use the bathroom, and hinted that Jackson—desperate to sleep—may have self-administered the final, fatal dose of Propofol while Murray was out of the room.
*   **On Murray's Intentions:** 
    Chernoff emphasized that Murray loved Jackson as a friend and was only trying to help him prepare for his upcoming "This Is It" concert tour. He insisted Murray was not a "fly-by-night" doctor hiding evidence, but a dedicated professional being unfairly vilified by the media and police.

---

### **Outcome Context**
Despite Chernoff's defense arguments, the items seized during these raids—particularly the shipping records proving Murray had ordered vast quantities of Propofol sent to his girlfriend's house—proved critical for prosecutors. In 2011, Conrad Murray was convicted of involuntary manslaughter and sentenced to four years in prison.

Following the death of Michael Jackson on June 25, 2009, law enforcement agencies—including the LAPD, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), and local police—executed search warrants on Dr. Conrad Murray’s offices and properties in **Houston, Texas**, and **Las Vegas, Nevada**, as well as a storage unit in Las Vegas in July 2009. 

The search warrants were part of a homicide investigation that ultimately led to Murray’s conviction for involuntary manslaughter. Here is what investigators found and seized during those raids:

### 1. Evidence of Massive Propofol Purchases and Shipping Records
The most critical evidence uncovered at Murray's offices and through related searches was the paper trail regarding **Propofol** (a powerful surgical anesthetic) and other sedatives. 
* Investigators found **invoices, shipping manifests, and receipts** showing that Murray had ordered vast quantities of Propofol from a pharmacy in Las Vegas (Applied Pharmacy Services). 
* Records revealed that between April and June 2009, Murray had ordered over **15,000 milligrams of Propofol**, along with midazolam and lorazepam. 
* The shipping records showed these powerful hospital-grade drugs were being delivered directly to the Santa Monica apartment of Murray's girlfriend, Nicole Alvarez, as well as his Las Vegas clinic, rather than to a medical facility or hospital.

### 2. Controlled Substances and Medical Supplies
At his Las Vegas office and a nearby storage locker, officers seized various medical supplies and prescription medications, including:
* Vials of **Propofol** and various benzodiazepines (Valium, Lorazepam, Midazolam).
* Medical paraphernalia used for administering IVs, such as saline bags, IV tubing, and needles.
* Flumazenil (a drug used to reverse the effects of sedatives).

### 3. Electronic Evidence and Communication Devices
Investigators seized hardware to analyze Murray's communications before and after Jackson’s death:
* **Computers and hard drives:** Contained medical files, billing information, and emails related to Michael Jackson's care and the "This Is It" concert tour promoter, AEG Live.
* **Cellular phones and flash drives:** These allowed investigators to construct a precise timeline of the morning Jackson died. Phone records proved Murray was making personal calls, sending text messages, and emailing during the crucial period when Jackson was heavily sedated under his care.

### 4. Financial Records
Authorities seized bank records, tax filings, and legal notices that revealed Murray was in severe financial distress.
* The search yielded documents showing **hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt**, unpaid student loans, child support arrears, and tax liens.
* *Significance:* Prosecutors later used these findings to establish a motive, arguing that Murray's desperate need for the $150,000-a-month salary offered by AEG Live caused him to compromise medical ethics and Jackson's safety to keep his famous client happy.

### 5. Medical Records Under Pseudonyms
Investigators found medical records related to Jackson's treatment, some of which were filed under Jackson's known pseudonyms (such as "Omar Arnold") or kept mixed in with unrelated patient files.

***

### Summary of Impact
The evidence seized during these raids—specifically the **shipping records for Propofol** and the **cell phone logs**—formed the backbone of the prosecution's case. It proved that Dr. Murray was acting far outside the standard of care by administering a hospital-only anesthetic in a residential home without proper monitoring equipment, leading to his 2011 conviction for involuntary manslaughter.

**POLICE SEARCH DR. CONRAD MURRAY’S OFFICES AS MICHAEL JACKSON MANSLAUGHTER PROBE INTENSIFIES**

**By CNN Staff**  
*(Updated July 2009)*

**LOS ANGELES (CNN)** — The criminal investigation into the sudden death of Michael Jackson has zeroed in on his personal physician, Dr. Conrad Murray, as federal agents and Los Angeles police execute a series of search warrants in what authorities are now treating as an involuntary manslaughter probe.

Law enforcement sources close to the investigation tell CNN that LAPD detectives, alongside agents from the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA), are attempting to piece together the final hours of the "King of Pop" and determine whether reckless medical malpractice led to his demise on June 25 at his rented Holmby Hills mansion.

At the epicenter of the growing legal storm is Dr. Murray, the 56-year-old cardiologist hired by concert promoter AEG Live to care for Jackson as he prepared for his 50-date comeback tour in London.

---

### **Evidence Seized in Multi-State Raids**

In recent days, joint task forces have raided Dr. Murray’s Global Cardiovascular Health Institute in Houston, Texas, as well as his residence and medical offices in Las Vegas, Nevada. Armed with search warrants targeting evidence of manslaughter and controlled substance violations, federal and local authorities spent hours combing through his facilities.

According to search warrant affidavits made public, officers seized a vast array of physical and digital evidence, including:

*   **Medical and Billing Records:** Files specifically related to Michael Jackson, as well as documents stored under various aliases allegedly used by the singer, such as "Omar Arnold."
*   **Digital Storage Devices:** Multiple computer hard drives, flash drives, and a cell phone used by Dr. Murray around the time of Jackson's death.
*   **Pharmaceutical Inventories:** Logs detailing the purchase, storage, and dispensation of controlled substances, specifically powerful sedatives and anesthetics.
*   **Communication Logs:** Emails, written correspondence, and phone logs between Dr. Murray, AEG Live executives, and Jackson's representatives.

Authorities are particularly interested in determining how large quantities of Propofol—a potent intravenous anesthetic typically restricted to hospital surgical settings—were acquired and transported to Jackson’s residence. 

---

### **Cherilyn Lee: Early Warnings About Propofol**

As investigators reconstruct Jackson's medical history, the testimony of Cherilyn Lee, a certified nurse practitioner and holistic nutritionist who treated Jackson earlier this year, has emerged as a critical element of the probe.

In an exclusive interview with CNN, Lee revealed that Jackson repeatedly begged her for Diprivan—the brand name for Propofol—in the months leading up to his death, claiming it was the only drug that could cure his debilitating insomnia.

"He told me, 'I just want to get some sleep. You don't understand, I want to be able to go to sleep,'" Lee recalled. "He was so exhausted."

Lee, who treated Jackson from January to May, said she adamantly refused his requests, warning the pop star of the deadly risks associated with administering surgical anesthetics outside a hospital without proper monitoring equipment.

"I told him, 'This medicine is not safe. It takes someone to monitor you while you're asleep. What if you don't wake up?'" Lee said. She noted that on April 21, a desperate Jackson told her that a doctor had assured him the drug was safe as long as he was monitored. 

Lee’s account provides prosecutors with potential evidence that Jackson was actively seeking the dangerous drug and that the severe risks of using Propofol at home were well-documented prior to Dr. Murray’s employment.

---

### **The Pending Toxicology Report: The Missing Puzzle Piece**

Despite the mounting physical evidence and witness testimony, the Los Angeles District Attorney’s Office has yet to file formal charges against Dr. Murray. Legal experts say prosecutors are waiting for the definitive finding: the Los Angeles County Coroner’s toxicology report.

Jackson’s autopsy was completed shortly after his death, but the official cause of death was deferred pending comprehensive toxicological testing. Analysts are performing complex chemical screens to determine the exact cocktail of drugs in Jackson's system at the time of death, as well as the precise dosages.

"The toxicology report is the linchpin of this entire case," said CNN legal analyst Sunny Hostin. "To secure a conviction for involuntary manslaughter, prosecutors must prove not only that Dr. Murray administered a lethal substance like Propofol, but that doing so constituted gross negligence that directly caused Jackson's death. The coroner's report will either prove or disprove that direct causation."

Sources indicate the coroner's findings are expected to be finalized within the coming weeks. If the toxicology report confirms acute Propofol intoxication compounded by other sedatives—and rules out suicide or accidental self-administration—charges against Dr. Murray could be filed swiftly.

---

### **The Defense Position**

Dr. Murray, who has retained Houston defense attorney Ed Chernoff, maintains that he did nothing wrong and did not prescribe or administer anything that should have killed the singer. 

Chernoff has publicly stated that Murray cooperated extensively with LAPD detectives during a lengthy, three-hour interview shortly after Jackson's death and did not hide any details. 

"Dr. Murray is not a runner," Chernoff said in a statement, emphasizing that his client remains devastated by Jackson's passing and is waiting for the truth to come to light. Defense representatives have cautioned against a "rush to judgment," suggesting that Jackson may have administered a fatal dose to himself while Murray was out of the room.

As the world awaits the coroner's final ruling, the LAPD's robbery-homicide division continues to interview physicians who previously treated Jackson, building a case that could soon culminate in one of the highest-profile medical manslaughter trials in American history.

*CNN's Special Investigations Unit contributed to this report.*
